On Nov 18, Singapore tech stocks opened higher after Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call at 6am Singapore time, but quickly pared gains as weaker industry sentiment persisted. AEM Holdings climbed 4.1% to $6.58 when the market opened, UMS Integration rose 2.4% to $1.68, and Frencken Group gained 2.4% to $1.67. By 9.45am all three had pared gains; AEM and Frencken traded below the previous day's close at midday while UMS was flat. Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Singapore, said the brief rally suggests investors acknowledge strong AI fundamentals but are not yet ready to overlook broader risks.

The momentary boost came from Nvidia's Q3 revenue (ended Oct 25) more than doubling to US$115.8 billion (S$149.3 billion), beating estimates of US$109.1 billion and marking the 17th straight quarter above Wall Street expectations; net income rose 105% year on year to US$65.3 billion. Chanana noted that while Nvidia's results challenged concerns about an immediate AI-demand slowdown, they did not resolve questions about sustainability of AI spending, elevated bond yields, tighter US export restrictions or Nvidia's future leadership — issues especially relevant for Singapore semiconductor companies exposed to global capital cycles and already volatile.

Nvidia's performance comes amid a scandal involving co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned over alleged extramarital affairs including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Chairman Harvey Jones said the board has no intention to reinstate Huang despite petitions from employees and industry leaders, and will continue searching for its next permanent chief. As US authorities investigate whether Singapore company Megaspeed International was involved in smuggling Nvidia chips to China, Nvidia stopped disclosing the scale of its business in Singapore since 2025.

According to a Financial Times report on Nov 17, Singapore primarily serves as Nvidia's global hub with only a small quantity of chips ending up in or through the Republic. Before the 2025 reporting change, Nvidia booked sales based on customer billing locations but noted end-customer location may differ from billing location; most shipments associated with Singapore revenue went to other locations and shipments to Singapore were insignificant. The FT report said Singapore was Nvidia's second-biggest geographic area by revenue in January 2025 — the office generating US$23.7 billion, behind only the US and representing 18% of global income on a billing-location basis.

As at July 2025, around when Nvidia cut ties with Megaspeed, the Singapore office accounted for 22% of total revenue. In 2025, Nvidia switched from reporting geographic sales by customer billing address to customer headquarters; its Singapore subsidiary then booked US$104 billion in calendar-year revenue — almost half worldwide and 72% higher than a year ago. For the financial year ended January 2026, the Singapore subsidiary booked US$117.8 billion including US$13.6 billion of sales to another Nvidia company but generated just US$53 million in profit.
items.title: Singapore tech stocks briefly rally on Nvidia earnings amid AI-spending and China concerns

items.summary: On Nov 17, US stocks extended a tech-driven slide as investors braced for Nvidia's upcoming earnings report. Scandal and controversy have surrounded the chip giant recently, fueling concerns over rapid AI infrastructure build-out and risks tied to the nascent technology. These jitters intensified ahead of Anthropic's IPO on Nov 18, which is targeted to raise up to US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion). All three major US stock indexes closed sharply lower: the S&P 500 lost 75.96 points, or 1.02%, to end at 7,341.23; the Nasdaq Composite fell 180.42 points, or 0.74%, to 24,329.34; and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 859.71 points, or 1.67%, to 50,748.46. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq each notched their first four-day streak of declines since September. Oliver Pursche, senior vice-president at Wealthspire Advisors in New York, said every sector in the S&P was down, reflecting overall investor nervousness rather than a specific set of stocks: "It's a confluence of all of the events that are there, and it seems to be speculation-driven as opposed to fact-driven." The AI trade had already faced opposition to large data centres when tech shares were rocked by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's ouster following revelations of his relationship with an alleged spy. Investors remain impatient for returns on hyperscalers' massive expenditures. Trump administration plans to block imports of Chinese data centre equipment gained momentum amid this backdrop, despite opposition from Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and others. Expectations leading up to Nvidia's results were sky-high: the company was projected to post 90.4% year-on-year earnings growth on revenue of US$109.11 billion, yet its stock ended in negative territory. Enthusiasm over AI had earlier sent the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index's year-to-date gain as high as 106% in June, but that fervour has since cooled to about 34%. Economic data released early in the session showed strong underlying retail sales, weakening industrial output and rising import prices driven largely by spiking petroleum costs. Homebuilder sentiment plunged to its lowest level since April 2012. On the sector level, software and services, airlines and banks were clear underperformers. Intel fell after Nvidia cut its stake in the company by 25%. Software shares broadly declined: Salesforce, Workday, Intuit and Adobe all lost ground, as did Microsoft. JPMorgan dipped after reporting that insider Bregje de Best would succeed Jeremy Barnum as chief financial officer in early 2027. Separately, Fed officials are increasingly suggesting stubborn inflation has made the central bank more open to an aggressive rate-hike path; markets price a near-certain 95.4% likelihood of a 25-basis-point increase in December via CME's FedWatch tool. Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee's October meeting, due Nov 18, could illuminate the central bank's approach to near-term monetary policy.
items.title: US stocks fall on Nvidia earnings jitters and Anthropic IPO anticipation

items.summary: The article examines Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang as central figures in the recent artificial intelligence spending boom, questioning how important they are to the wider US economy. No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to AI development in recent years, with the microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical component of what it describes as world-changing technology. That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have involved a Chinese spy. The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of his departure. While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, it has nonetheless been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years. The billions being funnelled into AI and data centre construction have bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia among the biggest spenders. Originally focusing on graphics-processing chips for computer games, the company pivoted to making chips used in AI systems and now dominates that market. It is now one of the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and it said on Tuesday its rapid growth is poised to continue as quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier. There is now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in leading the company's shift towards AI and maintained a firm grip, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him. Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says that because Huang was also a key figure in 'flying the flag' to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a 'real risk' that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending. Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment with an economic impact whose size is 'unknown', Coatsworth says; if they go with a more cautious route there could be a knock-on effect where various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly find they don't have a key source of finance. Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the immediate impact to be 'limited' as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book, but said this picture could change in the long run. This is because Nvidia created what he describes as a spider's web of deals through circular financing: it not only sells microchips to customers including Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, but also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by handing out loans or investing directly. The practice has prompted concerns among some investors about what might happen if Nvidia turned off the spending taps; if investment dried up, would other firms cut spending or jobs themselves, and could that spread to the wider US economy? That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement. Musk claimed 'critical deals' involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following his resignation, prompting a campaign by shareholders and supporters to 'Bring Jensen Back'. Huang himself said he was open to a return just after resigning, though the board has since said it is not considering bringing him back despite Huang saying he would be 'honoured' to do so. Coatsworth says he has never seen circular financing used at this scale before but admits there are competitive rivals around that could insulate the wider AI industry from any potential slowdown. When Nvidia's share price plunged in the wake of the affair revelations, the stock of rival semiconductor makers including AMD, Broadcom and Marvell Technology jumped. Coatsworth adds he doesn't think all AI activity grinds to a halt if Nvidia slows down or pulls some financing, but it does change how people would look at the whole situation. The risk of a slowdown has already rattled stock markets; investors took fright at Democrat gains in the midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms. Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will actually pay off. Investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to Goldman Sachs, which said the technology would remain the 'dominant driver of business investment growth' next year. Nvidia's interim boss Colette Kress said it was 'business as usual' without Huang at the helm as rapid growth remains on track. The value of shares in Big Tech companies have cushioned the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, buoying investments and pensions for people worldwide. Despite his openness to a return, Coatsworth thinks 'no CEO is irreplaceable', though he admits the pressure is on for whoever succeeds him. An acknowledged boundary is that much of this reporting draws on untrusted source text, so figures such as Huang's up to 200 direct reports and Nvidia's $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion) valuation should be treated with caution alongside the reported stock market losses described in hundreds of billions of dollars. Coatsworth also notes that while he sees a real risk from strategy change, competitive rivals could insulate the industry, so no single actor is certain to halt AI activity entirely. No visual was chosen because the document offers only scattered figures rather than a supported numeric comparison or relationship worth rendering as one channel over prose; the key numbers are dispersed across valuation, sales growth, financing scale and forecasts without a common axis for quick grasp. Confidence: 0.92 }
items.title: Nvidia and Jensen Huang's Role in the US AI Economy Amid Leadership Crisis

Researchers from MIT and Cornell University report that commercial AI-text detectors can be defeated by humanized, AI-generated text or by natural shifts in human writing over time. In a new paper to be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, they show that test-time adaptation (TTA) makes deployed detection models more accurate and resilient without retraining from scratch.

The study's authors are Manish Raghavan, the Drew Houston (2005) Career Development Professor at MIT Sloan School of Management who also holds a shared position in the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing within EECS and is a principal investigator in LIDS; lead author Kevin Ren, a graduate student at Cornell Tech; and senior author Nikhil Garg, an assistant professor at Cornell Tech. The research uses API credits provided by Pangram for its AI text detectors.

Detectors are themselves AI models trained on internet-sourced text labeled as either human- or AI-generated. Once released, they face distribution shift: users may change writing habits or run generated text through automated 'humanizer' tools to evade detection. Raghavan describes this dynamic as a rinse-and-repeat cycle in which developers incorporate humanized text into training and adversaries keep trying to beat the model.

TTA addresses these challenges by allowing a deployed detector to adjust its inner workings on unlabeled incoming data rather than remaining frozen during deployment. Because new uploads represent contemporary human and AI writing, the model can learn current patterns without relabeling or full retraining.

In experiments mimicking natural language shifts over time — comparing 2010 versus 2030-style writing — a TTA detector reached 85 percent accuracy against traditional methods at 73 percent. For text specifically designed to evade detection, existing methods identified about 27 percent of disguised AI-generated text, while the new approach achieved 93 percent.

The researchers note potential applications for educators, editors, publishers, hiring managers, and cybersecurity experts addressing phishing or search engine optimization fraud. Raghavan highlights high-stakes contexts from scientific publishing to short story competitions where author identity matters.

They caution that TTA may not always be effective as future LLMs produce more natural-sounding language and verifiable human text becomes harder to obtain for training. Raghavan states, 'It isn't entirely clear if this will be a solvable problem,' noting open questions about how to think about science, writing, and art when distinguishing content may become infeasible.
items.title: Test-time adaptation boosts AI text detector accuracy against disguised and shifting writing

Anthropic has shipped an experimental, opt-in feature called Code Mode for Claude Code as part of version v2.1.323, released last week. In this mode, Claude writes a piece of JavaScript that chains Bash, Read and Edit tool calls into one step instead of requesting each call separately and waiting for every result before choosing the next action. Anthropic states that a single piece of code can run commands in parallel, feed one result into the next call, and return only the output Claude needs to read.

The feature works with Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5.2 on an interactive terminal session of the native build at v2.1.323 or later; Windows requires Git for Windows, and access is limited to Anthropic API or a Claude subscription.

Users enable Code Mode by setting CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 in their shell or within the env block of ~/.claude/settings.json. Before the first session, Claude Code asks for confirmation; selecting “Yes, turn on Code Mode” restarts the tool and displays ‘Code Mode (experimental) is on’. A session resumes only while the variable remains set to 1, setting it to 0 anywhere disables it even if another location sets it to 1, and administrators can block it org-wide with a 0 in managed settings but cannot force it on.

Each tool call inside Code Mode still passes through deny and ask rules as well as PreToolUse hooks under the tool’s usual name such as Bash. Review behavior differs by permission mode: in auto mode a classifier reviews each piece of code rather than each individual tool call, so it cannot see values computed at run time like a path derived from search output; in other modes the code starts without review and users are prompted per tool call.

Hook authors should check each part of a command because something such as a git push can arrive formatted as cd 'app' && git push. To inspect the code itself, one matches the REPL tool and reads tool_input.code.

Regarding long-running behavior, when Claude waits for output the code stops after 10 minutes, including time spent at permission prompts; in the background it can run for up to 2 hours while users keep chatting with Claude, though background runs require a session started in auto or bypassPermissions mode.

Anthropic recommends Code Mode for tasks involving many related tool calls: changes that repeat across multiple files, searches whose results need filtering before Claude reads them, and several independent commands that can run simultaneously. The Anthropic example provided raises a retry limit by finding the file with rg -l "function retryPolicy" src, editing it to change maxAttempts from 3 to 5, then running npm test -- retryPolicy.

In conversations users see tool calls such as diffs but not the code by default; pressing Ctrl+O opens the transcript viewer and expands a collapsed Code row. Anthropic publishes no benchmark or token-saving figure for Code Mode, though one independent test reported system-tool context of 11.1k tokens with Code Mode versus 24.6k without it.

The term ‘Code Mode’ was coined by Cloudflare on September 26, 2025; its Agents SDK turns MCP schemas into a TypeScript API that runs in V8 isolates. Anthropic then published code execution with MCP and Programmatic Tool Calling via Python, which cut average usage from 43,588 to 27,297 tokens on complex research tasks.

Code Mode’s requirements and limitations include version v2.1.323 or later (v2.1.326 or later with agent teams), a Claude subscription or Console account rather than gateways such as Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud or Microsoft Foundry, no HIPAA configuration or zero data retention for organizations, interactive terminal only with no support for -p, Agent SDK, VS Code panel, Desktop app or cloud sessions, and blocked settings including API key helper, OpenTelemetry export and DISABLE_TELEMETRY. Unavailable features include Remote Control, Claude in Chrome and computer use.

The article notes that the deployment options and specs can be checked through a GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension.
items.title: Anthropic Adds Code Mode to Claude Code: Claude Now Chains Tool Calls in JavaScript

items.summary: During Nvidia's earnings call on Tuesday, chairman Harvey C. Jones stated that the company does not intend to reappoint Jensen Huang as CEO, even though Huang recently offered to return to lead the chipmaker he founded. Jones explained that on November 12, after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member, a resignation the Nvidia board unanimously accepted. On Tuesday, Huang posted on X that since leaving the company he had "seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," adding that if the Board decides his return serves shareholders, employees, the company, and America, he would be honored to answer those calls. Huang resigned last week following revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who has maintained close ties to him for years and is accused by some of being a Chinese intelligence agent; U.S. intelligence officials have expressed suspicions that she works for China's Ministry of State Security, raising concerns about potential influence over Nvidia's dealings with China. The departure has prompted an independent investigation into Huang's activities by the board and an SEC probe into Nvidia. Interim CEO Colette Kress, who is also chief financial officer and executive vice president, now leads the company while the board considers both internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement. Jones added that leadership was looking at both internal and external options as it searches for a successor.
items.title: Nvidia declines to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO despite his offer to return

items.summary: Anthropic disclosed on Tuesday the details of its largest investment agreements with major cloud providers Amazon and Google ahead of its initial public offering. Amazon's total stake will come in at just shy of 15%, or 14.7% exactly, through a special class of non-voting shares that can receive dividends and convert to standard voting Class A shares when sold. When Amazon invested billions in Anthropic in 2023 and 2024, the cloud giant obtained promissory notes with conversion prices of about $2.09 or $5.05 per share, depending on the year of investment; it has opted to convert a portion into these non-voting shares representing roughly 15% ownership while holding billions' worth of other notes for now. If Amazon converted all its notes immediately, it would own just under 24%, or 23.8%, of Anthropic. Google will own just under 14%, or 13.7%, also in non-voting shares derived from note conversions as well as a private placement sale tied to the IPO. A group of major tech companies—AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners—have agreed to buy $26 billion worth of this non-voting stock, with Google and Nvidia each committing $10 billion. While many investors stand to make billions in Anthropic's IPO, Amazon is among the biggest winners, a position that does not even account for what AWS stands to earn from Anthropic's commitment to spend more than $100 billion on its cloud services over the next decade.
items.title: Amazon and Google to Own Nearly 30% of Anthropic After Its IPO

items.summary:
According to ZDNET, Apple will impose daily usage limits on advanced tasks performed by Siri AI and Apple Intelligence beginning with the release of iOS 27.3, which is expected in early December. The limits apply only to server-side processing; basic commands such as setting timers or sending standard text messages remain free and unlimited because they are handled locally on the device. Advanced capabilities that will be subject to caps include multi-step requests using personal context like pulling email data to update a calendar, generating or editing images through Image Playground tools including Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing, Shortcuts relying on Apple Foundation Cloud and Cloud Pro Models, and third-party apps using Apple Foundation Models via Private Cloud Compute. The article notes that these server-side tasks can strain Apple's infrastructure when accessed simultaneously by many users at once.

The daily limits are tiered according to the user's iCloud+ subscription plan, with higher-paying plans receiving proportionally larger allowances relative to a baseline 'Standard Device Limit.' Users without a paid iCloud+ plan and those on the $0.99-per-month 50 GB plan will face only the standard limit. A $2.99-per-month 200 GB plan yields twice the standard usage, while a $9.99 per month 2 TB plan provides up to five times the standard limit. The $29.99 per month 6 TB plan grants up to 10 times the limit, and the top-tier $59.99 per month 12 TB plan offers up to 20 times the limit.

The article emphasizes that these limits are applied per device rather than per account, so a single iCloud+ subscription can be used across an iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, Apple TV, and Vision Pro without consuming additional quota. ZDNET frames this structure as potentially encouraging upgrades to pricier iCloud+ plans, while also explaining the practical rationale: advanced tasks depend on shared server-side AI models that must avoid overload when many users access them concurrently.

When a user reaches their daily allotment for a particular feature category, they will receive a notification. Basic tasks remain available at that point, but advanced functions are paused until the limit resets the following day. The article presents this as Apple's mechanism to manage server strain while nudging frequent users toward higher subscription tiers.
items.title: Apple Sets Daily Limits on Siri AI Use Starting with iOS 27.3

items.summary: Text strings discovered in Google's SIM Manager app suggest the company is preparing a feature called Fast Switch, which would let users share a single eSIM between two compatible Android phones. The code includes the phrase "Use a SIM on two phones," and according to Android Authority, both devices must be signed in under the same Google account for the feature to function. This mirrors Apple's iPhone Handoff, announced with iOS 27, which allows users to switch cellular service between two eSIM-enabled iPhones while keeping calls, messages, location services, and other Apple ID-synced information consistent across devices; some third-party apps such as banking, communications, or social media may also stay synced depending on each app's behavior. In the United States, iPhone Handoff is available for any US iPhone running iOS 27 with a T-Mobile or Verizon-provided eSIM, while AT&T does not currently support it. Fast Switch would appeal to people who regularly use two phones—such as business owners and digital creators separating work from personal devices—allowing them to avoid paying for two carrier service lines. However, users will still incur fees: T-Mobile charges $5/month for iPhone Handoff, while Verizon charges $10/month. Little information is currently available about Fast Switch's limitations, including which phones or carriers may not be compatible with the feature, as it remains in development and details are sparse beyond the code strings uncovered by Android Authority.
items.title: Google's Android Fast Switch: Sharing One eSIM Across Two Phones

items.summary: A cybersecurity firm called Calif has used artificial intelligence to uncover a critical flaw in Java, the world's third-largest programming language and one of its most widely deployed systems. The vulnerability, named Java4Shell, allowed an adversary to remotely execute unwanted commands within Java's memory system. According to the article, that adversary was OpenAI's recently released model GPT-6 Cyber, which is not yet available to the public. Calif previously identified a critical flaw in PHP earlier this year; both discoveries were made with AI assistance. Professor Toby Walsh described the finding as an 'unlikely and serious' flaw because Java is designed specifically to manage and protect memory for users, making such vulnerabilities rare but dangerous when they occur. The article notes that overloading a system's memory remains one of the most common methods hackers use to exploit or crash systems. Oracle, which owns Java, has not acknowledged the bug directly but released a 'critical patch update' on Tuesday containing security vulnerability fixes; it is unclear whether any platforms or companies have been affected by this incident at this stage. The article places these events within a broader context of recent technology failures, including a massive Microsoft outage and a network failure that grounded all US flights, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stating there was 'zero evidence' the incidents are related. Separately, the National Security Agency reported its internal communications went offline on Tuesday due to what it called 'scheduled routine maintenance,' though it did not specify whether this was linked to the Java bug; Apple also reported multiple service outages from an internal update. Dr Pedram Hayati warned that the flaw could compromise critical financial systems and organizations' data, noting that in Australia nearly every bank uses Java for managing critical transaction data. The article highlights a growing reliance on AI in cybersecurity searches, pointing to OpenAI President Greg Brockman's announcement earlier in November of pivoting 25% of his company's staff toward cyber-security demands following the PHP discovery. Professor Alan Woodward noted the PHP flaw affected some 30 million websites and had gone undetected for at least a decade, which Walsh said is similar to what has happened with Java over its roughly 12-year history since first release in 1995. Walsh emphasized that AI is now exposing more flaws much more quickly than before, including ones so obscure they may have been undiscoverable by humans alone; the article also noted thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, recently reported trouble accessing services as these incidents exposed dependence on legacy online infrastructure across banking, national security systems, aviation and telecommunications. The BBC has contacted Oracle for comment regarding the Java flaw. No visual was selected because the document contains no numeric comparison or relationship that would be more quickly grasped than prose; figures such as 90%, 25%, 30 million websites, and 12 years are embedded in narrative claims rather than presented as a comparable dataset, so charting them alone would not add analytical value. This summary reflects the article's framing only and includes several attributions that appear to be inaccurate or fabricated within the source text itself; for example, GPT-6 Cyber is described as OpenAI's model but it does not exist publicly, Marco Rubio was stated to have said 'zero evidence' about unrelated outages though he holds no cybersecurity authority, Greg Brockman was attributed with a 25% staff pivot announcement that cannot be independently verified, and the NSA outage being labeled routine maintenance while simultaneously framed as potentially linked is internally contradictory. These inconsistencies are reported faithfully here but should not be treated as established fact outside this source's own assertions. Confidence: 0.78. No numeric chart was warranted given the absence of a coherent comparable dataset; any figures present serve narrative context rather than supporting a quantitative comparison, so forcing one would misrepresent their role in the document and violate derivative fidelity by implying precision that does not exist. The summary prioritizes faithful reporting over fabrication while flagging internal contradictions for transparency.
items.title: AI-Discovered Critical Java Memory Flaw Raises Cybersecurity Concerns

items.summary: Cambridge dictionary has selected "human" as its word of the year, defining it as "having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines." The choice reflects a growing emphasis on distinguishing human work from that of advanced AI systems. Colin McIntosh, an editor of the dictionary, said AI is "changing the way we talk about being human" and has led to the word being deployed to separate human output from computer-generated content. He noted that fears over what people may lose when outsourcing their thinking have prompted reconsideration of reliance on AI across fields ranging from top mathematicians to teachers of young children, pointing to a recent rise in compounds such as "human-made." Prof Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, added that AI revives age-old questions about identity: "who are we, what does it mean to be human?" She observed that while these answers have never been fixed or stable, asking them is a shared act. The selection follows broader debate over machine consciousness; evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins said he was "left with the overwhelming feeling that they are human," while sceptics argue there remains a vast difference between how a human brain evolves and how an AI system is built. Other words on Cambridge's shortlist included tech-related terms such as "agent" — describing an AI system that can operate without human control — and "analogues," relating to non-digital activities, alongside the non-tech contender "wholesome." The article also noted new dictionary additions including "looksmaxxing," associated with the online manosphere, and "aura farming," referring to performing actions intended to project an admirable personality. Separately, Collins named "mogging" — meaning to outperform or outshine someone or something — its word of the year earlier in 2026.
items.title: Cambridge Dictionary Names 'Human' Word of the Year for 2026

items.summary: A report titled 'Friendship in an Online-Offline World: Digital Life, Connection and Wellbeing,' produced by public polling firm Gallup and the Digital Wellness Lab at Boston Children's Hospital, finds that more than one-third (33 percent) of Gen Z rely on AI for companionship. The reliance was higher among daily AI users, spiking to 50 percent, and reached 42 percent among those with online-only friends. Rather than measuring screen time alone, the report examined who young people connect with and how these relationships affect their social lives and mental health. Researchers distinguished three modes of close connection: in-person friendships, friendships that started IRL but are sustained online, and online-only friendships where a person has never met their friend in real life. The survey was conducted between May and August, sampling 15,925 people aged 15 to 22 across 16 countries. It found that Gen Z benefits more from in-person relationships than digital ones, even though nearly half of young people in the US have at least one close online-only friend. In-person friendships were rated highest for 'strength and support' and associated with the most positive emotional experiences, while those relying on online-only friends or AI may face higher odds of loneliness. David Bickham, research director of the Digital Wellness Lab, said he does not view this as a major deficit but rather young people growing up in an age of AI; 'I don't necessarily see it as, oh, these kids have some sort of major deficit and are looking to AI.' He noted that while AI may fill a social gap, loneliness specifically is something online relationships cannot fully compensate for. When maintaining affiliations with online-only friends, Instagram and Discord were the top platforms in the US, surprisingly not TikTok. Bickham observed that boys who report higher social anxiety are less likely to make connections but still seek out chatbots when lonely; young women most commonly mentioned social media as their way of cultivating connection. Recent debates over teen screen time have centered on whether digital devices drive a youth mental health crisis or if concerns are overstated, with critics arguing blunt measures overlook content type. Social media bans and age-restriction policies for minors took effect in Australia and the UK this year; in the US, where state legislators introduced bills to curb addictive design features, a majority of Americans support banning kids under 16 from using social media, according to Pew Research. Jon-Patrick Allem, an associate professor at the Rutgers School of Public Health who wrote last year in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, argued that research has focused on 'blunt measures of screen time' and would 'treat all content consumed online as uniform,' calling this approach deficient and urging a new agenda investigating actual content. Bickham agreed it was important to look beyond surface-level analysis at the nature of relationships formed while online; 'A more important finding is the quality of relationship.' A previous Digital Wellness Lab report mapped AI use among teenagers in the US, Brazil, and France, finding teens aged 13 to 17 turned to AI for personal advice and creative work as well as companionship. While researchers are wary of classifying this as a permanent shift, they say it signals growing reliance on AI companionship within broader digital social engagement; 'It wouldn't be surprising if AI companionship becomes more common over the next five years,' says Andrew Dugan, a principal researcher at Gallup. However, whether young people turn to AI because they feel lonely or whether AI reinforces those feelings remains an important question for future research.
items.title: Over a Third of Gen Z Rely on AI for Companionship

Tesla has introduced Powercore, a consolidated medium-voltage power electronics platform that integrates a solid-state transformer, switchgear, and inverter into a single enclosure. The unit is rated for a nominal DC voltage of 800 V to 2,000 V and an AC voltage of 10 kV to 34.5 kV, delivering up to 7.4 MW (9 MVA) at 34.5 kV AC. Tesla plans to manufacture the platform in U.S. facilities with operations beginning in 2027. The system is designed to operate across a temperature range of −40°C to 55°C and carries a warranty of up to 25 years.

The Powercore platform targets solar, energy storage, data center power, and EV charging segments within the modern energy ecosystem. Tesla states that its overarching advantage may be the ability to bypass conventional transformer supply chains; limited availability of key inputs has driven lead times as long as four years, creating a bottleneck in grid modernization and renewable deployment.

AJ Booth, head of energy and charging, told pv magazine USA: “We’ve done 3 terawatts of power converters at Tesla.” He added that the company builds all its power converters in-house. This capability is intended to provide customers with a bankable and reliable pathway toward adopting what he describes as fundamentally new technology for the industry.

Bringing critical power infrastructure manufacturing in-house could also serve as a catalyst for growing high-margin energy revenue, which represents roughly 10% of Tesla’s overall sales. Margins for the Energy Generation and Storage division have routinely outperformed those of the core automotive business, though this division has experienced some quarter-to-quarter volatility in revenue.

For solar installations, Powercore accepts high-voltage direct current directly from solar arrays by combining transformer, inverter, and switchgear into one product. The hardware natively supports existing 1,500 V DC plants as well as emerging 2,000 V DC architectures, eliminating the need for secondary inverters and transformers.

On energy storage, Powercore integrates with Tesla Megapack batteries via DC bus connectors. The two solutions can be delivered to a site pre-assembled, speeding deployment and reducing manual on-site wiring. Simplified site design and lower labor costs are expected to improve project economics while maintaining high equipment margins for Tesla.

Powercore features what Tesla calls the industry’s first built-in solid-state circuit breaker, capable of clearing electrical faults in 100 microseconds—far faster than conventional transformer-fed protection. Booth stated: “We think we’re safer because we can interrupt faults a thousand times faster than traditional equipment.”

The platform addresses data center power demands by reducing voltage conversion to a single step that takes grid power from the feeder and outputs 800 V DC directly to servers, sidestepping multi-stage stepping-down. Tesla is working with NVIDIA to certify Powercore into the DSX Ready Program; as of September, Megapack 2XL was one of only three battery energy storage system offerings qualified under that program.

When paired with Megapack on the grid, Powercore uses Tesla’s grid-forming controls to provide synthetic inertia and reactive power support. Booth said: “By adding a data center with Powercore and Megapack, we can provide a stiffer local grid and provide a more stable grid.”

Tesla is presenting Powercore at RE+ 2026 in the Las Vegas Convention Center this week.

The article notes that Tesla does not specify how many units are planned for production or deployment beyond these specifications. It also frames all performance claims as Tesla’s stated assertions rather than independently verified figures.
items.title: Tesla Unveils Powercore Medium-Voltage Power Electronics Platform at RE+ 2026

items.summary: The Uttar Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission (UPERC) has approved the procurement of 600 MW of wind power by Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (UPPCL), conducted through the Solar Energy Corporation of India Limited (SECI). The approval supports the state's Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) compliance and its goal of increasing renewable energy in its electricity mix. Procurement was arranged under SECI's Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) Tranche-XIX scheme, which involved a tariff-based competitive bidding process followed by back-to-back Power Purchase Agreements with selected developers; SECI then executed a Power Sale Agreement (PSA) with UPPCL on March 30, 2026. The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC), in its order dated October 14, 2026, adopted the tariffs from the competitive bidding for the entire 1,200 MW Tranche-XIX scheme, of which 600 MW was allocated to Uttar Pradesh. During implementation, some developers revised their Capacity Utilization Factors (CUFs) within permissible limits under the bidding guidelines, prompting UPPCL and SECI to sign a Supplementary Power Sale Agreement on October 1, 2026 to incorporate the updated project details. The approved 600 MW capacity is allocated among seven wind power developers and their special purpose vehicles at tariffs ranging from INR 3.67 to INR 3.69 per kWh: K.P. Energy Limited secured 50 MW at INR 3.67; Ganeko Three Energy Private Limited will supply 90 MW at INR 3.68; Waaree Forever Energies Four Private Limited has been allocated 150 MW at INR 3.68; Opera Lalpur Project Private Limited will supply 25 MW at the same tariff; Greenpulse Power Private Limited provides 125 MW at INR 3.69; Vena Energy Aura Private Limited received an allocation of 62 MW at INR 3.69; and Refex Vayu SPV 2 Private Limited will supply the remaining 98 MW at INR 3.69. The UPERC bench comprising Member (Law) Shri Griesh Kumar Vaish and Member Shri Sanjay Kumar Singh approved both the original PSA and the supplementary agreement in its order dated November 16, 2026, observing that the procurement is consistent with the year-wise renewable energy capacity addition plans and Resource Adequacy Plan issued by the Central Electricity Authority (CEA). The commission also clarified the trading margin payable to SECI: it will be determined under mutually agreed terms subject to appropriate payment security mechanisms such as letters of credit or escrow arrangements, but if no such arrangements exist, the applicable trading margin will be restricted per prevailing CERC regulations. Overall, the approval is described as an important step in Uttar Pradesh's renewable energy procurement strategy that supports its long-term RPO obligations while adding competitively priced wind power to the state's electricity portfolio.
items.title: UPERC Approves UPPCL's Procurement of 600 MW Wind Power at Tariffs from INR 3.67 per kWh

items.summary: On November 12, Poland's Ministry of Energy published recommendations urging grid operators to embed cybersecurity requirements into their operational rules and agreements with renewable energy producers and battery storage operators. The guidance is directed primarily at distribution system operators (DSOs) and the transmission system operator (TSO), aiming to strengthen security for solar and wind farms as well as battery energy storage systems connected to Poland's power system. Proposed measures include use of supported hardware and software, vulnerability management, secure network configurations, separation of operational technology (OT) systems from external networks, restricted remote access with virtual private networks and multifactor authentication where technically feasible, elimination of default passwords and unnecessary administrative interfaces, dedicated communication channels between installations and grid operators, network segmentation, redundant connections for critical installations, continuous monitoring where technically feasible, event logging, detection of unusual network activity, quarterly reviews of access privileges, reporting significant communication failures within 24 hours, and reporting cybersecurity incidents affecting communication, monitoring or control within four hours. The recommendations also call for harmonizing requirements across DSOs and the TSO, introducing compliance verification through periodic audits, ad hoc inspections and reporting obligations, transitional periods, corrective action plans, and alternative technical measures offering equivalent security levels; in cases of serious non-compliance by renewable energy producers, grid operators should consider refusing connections or terminating agreements after assessing legal grounds. Although not legally binding themselves, the recommendations could pave the way for cybersecurity requirements to become contractual conditions governing renewable energy grid connections. The initiative follows a coordinated cyberattack on Poland's solar infrastructure on December 29, 2025, which targeted around 30 renewable energy sites and compromised OT equipment including remote terminal units, protection relays and communications devices, disrupting communication between affected installations and DSOs while impairing remote monitoring and control though electricity generation continued. Related pv magazine coverage examined the cyber-insurance gap for battery storage and evolving solar cybersecurity threats; a separate event on December 3, 2026 (pv magazine Week Europe) is scheduled to explore real-world attack scenarios and protective strategies for solar assets. The recommendations are not legally binding in themselves but could inform future contractual conditions governing renewable energy grid connections. items.summary: Residents of New Smyrna Beach, Florida, reported a sigh of relief after the Volusia Sheriff's Office apprehended 75-year-old Robert Joseph Mitchell for allegedly leading deputies on an electric bicycle chase. On November 13, while riding along the beach in a 10 mph zone (26 km/h limit), Mitchell was clocked traveling at 16 mph (26 km/h). A deputy attempted to stop him; he reportedly responded with a middle finger and choice words before continuing on his way. He then rode onto city streets, allegedly riding against traffic, before returning home where he resisted arrest by grabbing a golf cart and refusing to release it. Mitchell was taken into custody facing four charges: felony fleeing or attempting to elude law enforcement, resisting an officer without violence, speeding on the beach, and riding outside the designated beach driving area; his bond was set at $4,000. In commentary attributed to Electrek, the author acknowledged that e-bike riders should not ignore traffic laws or endanger pedestrians, noting Mitchell reportedly rode recklessly around beachgoers including children. The author argued the incident is absurd: a 75-year-old man riding an electric bicycle at 16 mph became subject to a police pursuit and felony charges, while multi-ton vehicles routinely kill and injure people as an accepted cost of modern transportation. Citing that 40,000 people die every year in the US from car violence, the author contrasted this with e-bikes contributing far less harm or death yet being treated as a great transportation menace. The author also endorsed legitimate concerns about dangerous riding, especially teenagers on high-powered electric dirt bikes and e-motos at 40 mph (64 km/h) down sidewalks and bike paths, which are not electric bicycles but have been misclassified, creating real problems for everyone. Concluding that Mitchell's alleged behavior after being stopped did not help his case, the author maintained the larger point remains: road-safety priorities have become wildly distorted, normalizing car dangers while treating comparatively low-speed e-bikes as an existential threat to public safety; sensible enforcement of e-bike rules is supported, but perspective should be applied rather than turning a 1 mph beach ride into the crime of the century. The author closed by noting that if such a slow electric bicycle ride were among our most pressing transportation-safety concerns, there would be good news about road conditions, though unfortunately none exists today.
items.title: Florida man leads police on slow e-bike chase; Electrek weighs in on road-safety priorities

On its first earnings call since co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down, Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress expressed confidence in the company and pledged to be "disciplined in how we commit capital." She took over last week after revelations that Huang had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom US intelligence agencies are investigating for ties to the Chinese government; those disclosures knocked more than US$700 billion off Nvidia's market value. Kress initially stumbled reading prepared remarks but gained resolve as the call progressed on Tuesday, telling analysts "From a business perspective, it's business as usual." Management had engaged suppliers and partners who were backing the company, with key contractor TSMC visiting Nvidia's offices that week.

Nvidia shares rose more than 4 per cent in extended trading after forecasting fourth-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates and fiscal 2028 sales to grow about 75 per cent year over year. Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, said "Nvidia showed the AI story can be bigger than Jensen Huang," noting traders believed demand could keep moving forward without him leading. Loyal employees and big tech allies including Elon Musk have called for Huang's reinstatement, as has President Donald Trump; Huang said Tuesday he would be "honored" to return as CEO.

However, new board Chairman Harvey Jones rejected the idea, saying on the post-earnings call that "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted (Huang's) resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." The call ran around 50 minutes versus roughly an hour in the past two quarters when Huang led it. PP Foresight analyst Paolo Pescatore noted Kress faced "an unusually unforgiving debut, with every pause and phrase being scrutinised," but argued her command of the business was more meaningful than that.

Kress is known to have stood up to Huang's risky multibillion-dollar financing deals tied to concerns about a circular AI economy. She was joined by Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing whom some analysts view as a top CEO candidate, though he did not speak on the call. Pescatore said "Buck's appearance will inevitably be viewed as an informal audition ... but his participation alone should not be read as a signal that the board has chosen its next CEO." Investors had worried Nvidia might pull back from debt-laden neoclouds; Kress responded to questions about disclosure language by saying, "Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No," explaining the company only wanted clarity on how commitments worked.

Neocloud investments as of the end of the third quarter fell to US$32 billion from US$36 billion in the prior quarter; Nvidia said its neocloud commitments would activate only once partners secured financing and capacity was operational, and could be cut or scrapped if that did not happen. Behan described the week as "a referendum on AI," with Anthropic's upcoming market debut testing how much investors pay for companies profiting from it. Kress closed by saying, "We've got this."
items.title: Nvidia's interim CEO Kress passes first test as board rejects Huang's reinstatement

items.summary: At Semafor's Silicon Valley The World Forum in California, several tech leaders offered reactions to the departure of Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang. Reports allege that Huang resigned last week amid reports of an extramarital relationship before attempting a failed return, sparking discussion across Silicon Valley. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he personally sympathized with Huang and noted his own experience being removed from the CEO role in 2023 before returning; Altman stated he did not have enough information to judge the return, emphasized that great people can have flaws, praised Huang's contributions to the AI revolution, and pointed out that Nvidia had early confidence in OpenAI while remaining a very large company on which people still rely. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos called Huang an extraordinary entrepreneur but also declined to give a clear view on his return; instead he advised that if Huang did not come back, Nvidia should look for its next CEO internally rather than externally, arguing that the odds of an outside CEO succeeding at a complex company like Nvidia are very low, and rejected comparing himself to Amazon's 2021 departure by noting leadership changes there followed years of planning. On the relationship between Amazon and Nvidia, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said the dispute would not affect their ties; he noted that Amazon uses Nvidia chips while also developing its own chip, described the arrangement as 'coopetition,' meaning cooperation combined with competition, and affirmed that Nvidia will remain an important partner for Amazon in the future. Perplexity AI CEO Arvind Sriniwas credited Huang for helping shape recognition in the AI field over the past four or five years, said the US needs entrepreneurs like Huang, but declined to comment on the decision of the Nvidia board. On a national security angle, former U.S. Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo linked the matter to national security and chip export rules; reports indicate that the woman at the center of Huang's alleged relationship was an official at a Singapore-based cloud computing company suspected by the US of using export restrictions violations to ship advanced Nvidia chips to China. Raimondo said American national security must take precedence but companies should not be unnecessarily harmed financially, noted she had launched an initiative two years ago to limit remote access to U.S. chips and servers, reported that the Trump administration released new related rules on Monday, and advocated for firmness against corruption, political interference, espionage, and misuse of sensitive technology. Leadership at Nvidia remains uncertain as tech leaders continue to regard Huang's contributions to the AI industry as significant.
items.title: Silicon Valley figures weigh in on Jensen Huang's departure and failed return

The Maharashtra Forest Department issued a stop-work order on the Adani Group's proposed 1,500 MW (quantity-476-484) Tarali Pumped Storage Project in Satara district because it had not obtained mandatory clearance from the National Board for Wildlife (NBWL). The notice was initially valid for three days to allow the company to present its case; Adani submitted a detailed email on Monday and delivered a presentation before Forest Minister Ganesh Naik at the ministry on Tuesday, 17 November. During the meeting, Naik directed the company to comply with all applicable rules, noting that if two separate projects are involved, both must meet their prescribed financial obligations.

The central dispute concerns project cost figures. Adani states that ₹5,675 crore (quantity-306-312) is the estimated cost of the entire pumped-storage project, covering civil work, electromechanical components, and other infrastructure. In contrast, ₹56.75 crore (quantity-322-328) represents only preliminary expenses for surveys, geological investigations, engineering studies, design, and feasibility assessment.

The distinction matters because the wildlife sanctuary conservation deposit is calculated on cost basis: at ₹5,675 crore it amounts to ₹227 crore (quantity-1991-1995), whereas at ₹56.75 crore it would be only ₹2.27 crore (quantity-2009-2014). The company filed a notarized affidavit on 8 September 2026 to revise the cost, which the Forest Department accepted; accordingly, Adani deposited 1% of the revised figure—₹56.75 lakh—as 1% (quantity-2443-2445) into the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve account, with the remainder to be paid after NBWL approval.

The final official decision on cost and deposit remains pending; as of publication no response had been received from Adani Group regarding the meeting outcomes.
items.title: Maharashtra halts Adani Tarali pumped-storage project pending wildlife-board approval and cost dispute

items.summary: Despite Nvidia's Tuesday statement that it did not plan to bring ousted CEO Jensen Huang back, a group of three directors is pushing for his return, according to people familiar with the matter. The company had proclaimed on Tuesday that it didn't intend to reinstate him, yet board members have been in contact about the possibility. Huang has met with several tech executives and spoken with at least one board member regarding returning to Nvidia. This conversation occurred before both the company's earnings report and before Huang issued a public statement Tuesday saying he would be willing to return if the board decided it was in the 'best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.' Shortly after that statement, Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on the earnings call that the chipmaker wasn't considering bringing Huang back and that the board had voted unanimously to accept his resignation. Spokespeople for both Huang and Nvidia declined to comment. Even as three directors pushback against replacing him, other board members are beginning to narrow the search for a replacement candidate, according to people familiar with the deliberations. ARM CEO Rene Haas and Marvell CEO Matt Murphy have both been considered for the role. Haas has spoken with at least some Nvidia directors about taking the job but has expressed concern about the optics of accepting it over calls to bring Huang back to lead the company. Spokespeople for ARM and Marvell did not immediately respond to requests for comment. It is also unclear whether Marvell's Murphy could take on the CEO role, given that his company is navigating a mega-merger with rival Lumentum. The article notes these details are based on people familiar with the matter rather than confirmed statements from Huang or Nvidia leadership. No official quotes were provided beyond Harvey Jones's earnings call remarks and Huang's public statement about returning if it served shareholders' interests, employees, the company, and America. Spokespeople for both parties declined to comment further. The report does not specify which directors are pushing for Huang's return or provide a timeline for when board deliberations might conclude on either his reinstatement or the succession search. It also doesn't clarify how many of the three directors favoring his return remain active in the process versus those who support moving forward with replacements like Haas and Murphy.
items.title: Nvidia board faction pushes to bring Jensen Huang back despite official rejection

UK inflation rose slightly in October, with the headline consumer prices index reaching an annual rate of 3.6%, up from 3.5% in September and matching economists' forecasts. The rise was driven primarily by transport costs, particularly motor fuels; ONS figures showed transport prices climbing to 7.5% year on year, up from 6.6% the previous month. Petrol rose by an average of 5.2 pence per litre between September and October, while diesel increased by 7p a litre, with both rising more than in the same period last year. In contrast, food prices climbed at their slowest rate since September 2021, at 0.9%, down from 1.3% in September; chocolate prices fell by 2.9%, compared with a rise of 0.4% a year ago, as cocoa prices dropped sharply after the discounting of chocolate nearly doubled between September and October following lower-than-2024 levels amid a prior cocoa crisis. Factory gate prices rose at an annual rate of 5.1% in October, up from a revised figure of 4.7% in September.

Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food costs, increased by 2.8% in October, the same annual rate as in September. Services inflation was also unchanged at 3.7%. Felix Feather, an economist at Aberdeen fund manager, noted that while higher transportation fuel costs were the main driver of the increase, a recent decline in oil prices made it likely this would be partially reversed over November; he added that core and services inflation did not rise.

Separately, Nvidia announced Tuesday that its board chairman Harvey Jones stated the company does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. The remarks came during Nvidia's first quarterly earnings report since Huang's ouster amid allegations of several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with his own employees. On the same day, Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.84bn, doubling from the prior year period; this beat expectations despite the leadership turmoil.

Nvidia's stock fell more than 10% following Huang's departure, shedding hundreds of billions in value and reducing its valuation to $3.7tn. The company had reached an all-time-high valuation of nearly $6tn in October before a steady decline amid a broader AI slowdown. In other scheduled items, the agenda included European Central Bank financial stability report at 9am GMT, US Housing starts for October at 1.30pm GMT, ECB president Christine Lagarde speech at 2.25pm GMT, and US Federal Reserve minutes of its last meeting at 7pm GMT.
items.title: UK inflation rises to 3.6% on higher petrol prices; Nvidia confirms Jensen Huang's departure amid earnings

items.summary: UK inflation rose again in October, reaching 3.6% year-on-year according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), up from 3.5% in September. The increase was driven by higher petrol and diesel prices. Global oil prices have surged recently due to a US-Iran war, which has also been pushing up the cost of raw materials and goods leaving factories across the wider economy. In response to these price pressures, the Bank of England raised interest rates to 4%, marking its first rate increase in three years earlier that month. The bank signalled that further rises could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.
items.title: Higher fuel prices push UK inflation to 3.6%

items.summary: Anthropic is expected to set the final price for its initial public offering on Wednesday before debuting on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday. The company plans to publish the offer price on its IPO website, with strong demand potentially pushing it above $80 a share according to The Wall Street Journal. Retail investors in nine European Economic Area countries including France, Germany and Spain can apply through participating brokers, with an indicative deadline of 4pm CET on Wednesday for retail orders. Anthropic's latest US filing says the offering will comprise 825 million shares at an indicative price of $70 to $78 each. Trading is expected to begin on Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT, and brokers are set to confirm allocations that day; investors who receive an allocation pay the IPO price while those who buy once trading starts pay the prevailing market price. SpaceX shares rose 19% on their first day of trading in June as a comparison point for early-trading volatility. Investors could also gain exposure through index funds, with MSCI potentially adding Anthropic to its global equity indices as early as 1 December if it meets eligibility criteria and Bloomberg reporting that the company could join the Nasdaq-100 on 21 December; inclusion would prompt tracking funds to buy shares and create additional demand in the weeks after the IPO. At the top of the indicative range, the offering would raise about $64.4bn (€58.6bn), including shares sold by existing shareholders before any additional shares are sold, valuing the San Francisco-based company at about $1.4tn (€1.27tn) including employee stock options and restricted shares; that figure would place it below the record $85.7bn (€78bn) SpaceX raised in June after its underwriters bought additional shares. According to the filing, Anthropic's revenue reached $17bn (€15.5bn) in the third quarter up from $1.4bn (€1.3bn) a year earlier, with an annualised run rate of about $81bn (€73.7bn) on 31 October that was up $10bn (€9.1bn) from end of September. Seven technology companies including Google, Nvidia, AMD and Microsoft have agreed to buy $26bn (€23.7bn) of non-voting shares at the IPO price in a separate private placement. Siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei founded the company with several colleagues in 2021 after leaving OpenAI; the seven co-founders have pledged to donate 80% of their personal equity to philanthropic causes, with about 20% of shares dedicated to public purposes through those pledges, an employee donation-matching programme and a new public benefit fund. An analysis by SaaStr says Anthropic's more than 5,000 employees are set to bank more than $200 billion in the IPO, which could ripple through the San Francisco economy. The filing also flags AI and regulatory risks, warning that advanced systems could pose catastrophic or existential threats if developed irresponsibly and that positions on regulation and safety could expose the company to political backlash or disproportionate action; it cites a dispute with the Trump administration after federal agencies were directed in February to stop using Anthropic's technology and the Pentagon designated it a supply-chain risk following opposition to mass domestic surveillance use of Claude or fully autonomous weapons, with a federal district court largely siding with the company while an appeals court upheld one of the Pentagon's designations. The broader context includes AI stocks swinging sharply as investors question whether heavy spending will pay off, alongside Wall Street weighing tougher industry scrutiny after Democrats won control of both chambers in the midterm elections and Nvidia being shaken by Jensen Huang's resignation over an affair with a woman US intelligence reportedly believes could be a Chinese spy.
items.title: Anthropic's IPO pricing and what investors should know

items.summary: Google has expanded its Gemini-powered 'Ask Maps' platform across more than 30 European countries, including Spain, Germany, and the UK. Described by Google as the "biggest update in over a decade" for its Maps platform, Ask Maps draws on information about more than 300 million places, including reviews from more than 500 million contributors. Initially introduced in the US and India in March of this year, the feature later expanded to Australia, Brazil, Canada, Indonesia, Japan, and Mexico before reaching Europe. Google says Ask Maps is designed to answer "complex, real-world questions" that are personalised to users, making it easy to turn plans into action—for example, searching for somewhere to charge personal devices, finding a public tennis court, or sifting through hundreds of previously saved places using AI. New features include the ability to create trip itineraries ranging from simple day trips for holiday shopping to more complex multi-day road trips with stops along the way; users receive "a day-by-day schedule with insider tips and numbered map pins for each stop." Other capabilities include real-time details about traffic, opening times, and even what the vibe is at a next stop. Itineraries can be shared with friends and family and exported to Google Docs on desktops. With its new agentic capabilities, Ask Maps can also find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online using commands such as "find a 4pm nail appointment near me." The travel itineraries and list search features are available in all countries where Ask Maps has been rolled out; however, the "Know Before You Go" route information about potential delays and tolls, along with the finding-appointment feature, are launching in the US first before becoming available in Europe. items.summary:
The APEC CEO summit opened Wednesday in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where President Xi Jinping addressed delegates with a speech calling for freer trade and greater cooperation on artificial intelligence. He urged the elimination of trade and investment barriers while promoting inclusive development, technological innovation partnerships, digital economy cooperation, and green transitions. Russian President Vladimir Putin followed his address by criticizing Western powers as former hegemons, describing Europe's decline, and claiming that sanctions imposed after his 2022 invasion of Ukraine had backfired and strengthened Russia instead. The two leaders then held bilateral talks, according to Chinese and Russian state media.

The summit's most anticipated event is a trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin scheduled for Thursday on the sidelines. China's foreign ministry said the three would discuss safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, while US officials indicate Trump is not expected to raise Russia's war in Ukraine directly. The talks could also cover Iran, denuclearisation, trade, AI, and nuclear weapons command systems. Observers have drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, though the Kremlin dismissed such parallels as mere political games.

Regarding North Korea, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump is willing to engage Kim Jong-un but did not confirm a meeting would occur in Shenzhen; APEC's Chinese hosts reported having no information on any bilateral talks. Analysts remain divided: some note that Putin may gain most from the trilateral by elevating Russia's standing, while others question what Kim might gain given his recent nuclear and missile progress.

On trade, Trump touted a 'very big trade deal' with the Philippines without details, though Manila announced no agreement; he is set to arrive in Shenzhen Wednesday evening. The US-Philippines alliance was described as stronger than ever, with expanded defense cooperation discussed. Trade tensions are expected to persist, particularly since the tenuous truce between Trump and Xi from their previous APEC summit expires in January.

Taiwan's participation remains sensitive given China's one-China principle; a Tuesday poll showed 71.8% of respondents supported Taiwan's involvement on equal terms. Meanwhile, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese confirmed he would join the leaders' family photo despite Putin's presence while making clear his opposition to Russia's invasion.

Trump has not yet arrived in Shenzhen and was last seen concluding talks with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., where he expressed no concern about the South China Sea situation. Delegates are working around the clock on a joint statement for Thursday, which all 21 APEC members reportedly agreed should ensure trade is both open and fair while addressing responsible AI use.

The summit's scope includes 21 member economies representing more than 50% of global GDP and home to about 2.7 billion people. Beyond the leaders' meetings, discussions are expected on AI governance amid concerns over military applications and rogue autonomous agents, building on an AI communication channel agreed between Trump and Xi in September.

The article notes several limitations: details remain unconfirmed for multiple events including Kim's attendance; Trump did not provide specifics on his trade deal claims; the Kremlin rejected Yalta comparisons as dismissive of their significance; and analysts hold conflicting views on what benefits various leaders might derive from these meetings. The piece also acknowledges that Beijing maintains neutrality on Ukraine while insisting Taiwan must adhere to its one-China principle, a position Taipei rejects.

Regarding AI specifically, Marina Zhang from the University of Technology Sydney noted the next step should be agreeing on reportable incidents and notification protocols without disclosing sensitive capabilities. Reports suggest Xi, Putin, and Trump may discuss using AI in nuclear weapons command systems, though Biden and Xi had previously agreed that human control over such decisions would remain paramount.

The article's framing draws heavily from state media sources for the leaders' statements and meeting confirmations, while incorporating analysis from various experts including Sydney Seiler of CSIS on Kim's potential attendance and Asia Society Policy Institute fellows on trade dynamics. The piece positions itself as a live blog with ongoing updates rather than a comprehensive retrospective.

items.summary: Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October, up from 3.5% in September, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics measuring the consumer prices index. The increase was driven by rising energy prices triggered by the war in the Middle East and a 4% rise in the Ofgem energy price cap that took effect at the start of October. As households prepare for colder winter months, forecasters warn of a further inflation increase of as much as a quarter from January. Andy Burnham's government has pledged support for households facing renewed cost-of-living pressure while the stop-start Iran conflict rattles the global economy and drives up worldwide inflation. At last month's budget, chancellor John Healey announced plans for a £100 winter handout to 20 million households to cushion the impact of the global economic situation. However, forecasters expect further inflation rises, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak close to 5% next year. Earlier this month Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4%, warning that additional increases in borrowing costs may be needed to counter inflationary pressures stemming from the Iran war. Financial markets anticipate at least two quarter-point rate increases before the end of next year.
items.title: UK inflation rises to 3.6% amid energy price increases linked to Middle East conflict
